title: The AI Startup Landscape

thumbnail.headline: Where Can You Begin?
thumbnail.image: Navy background, a simple four-floor building in teal outline with the upper floors glowing, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Where Can You Begin?
slide.body: Simple icon of a four-floor building: ground floor grey (infrastructure), upper floors highlighted in teal (vertical AI, applications). Small tag: Building an AI Startup · Lesson 1.

production_notes: No facts to verify: all founders and companies are hypothetical, and the lesson states no statistics, prices or tool details (content.md Review Flags: None).
Amara (Ghana), Diego (Colombia) and Mei (Malaysia) are fictional. Stock footage must not show real company names, shop signs or logos.
The course has no business prerequisite: keep the definitions of startup, founder, MVP and model supplier on screen long enough to read.

Hook.voiceover: New AI companies appear all the time. Some build giant models that cost a fortune to train. Others build a simple app for one type of shop in one city. Both are called AI startups. So where could you realistically begin?

Explain.voiceover: Hi, and welcome to Building an AI Startup. You do not need any business training. We will explain every term as we go.

slide.title: The AI Startup Landscape
slide.body: Building an AI Startup · Lesson 1 of 15

Explain.voiceover: A startup is a young company that is still searching for a product that many customers want, and for a way to earn money from it that can grow. A founder is the person who starts the company.

slide.title: Two key words
slide.body: Startup: a young company still searching for a product many customers want, and a way to earn money that can grow. · Founder: the person who starts the company.

Explain.voiceover: Most startups move through five stages. First, an idea: a problem you want to solve. Second, validation: evidence that real people have this problem. Third, an MVP, or minimum viable product, the smallest product that tests your main idea with real users. Fourth, product market fit, when customers keep paying and tell others. Fifth, growth. This course covers the first three.

slide.title: The startup journey
slide.body: Five steps left to right: Idea → Validation → MVP (minimum viable product) → Product–market fit → Growth. The first three steps are highlighted with a bracket: 'This course'.

Explain.voiceover: AI startups can be grouped into four layers. Think of floors in a building. On the ground floor is infrastructure: companies that build large AI models, the chips that run them, or the data centres that host them. This floor needs huge amounts of money and computing power.

slide.title: Four layers of AI startups
slide.body: A four-floor building drawn bottom up. Ground floor highlighted: Infrastructure (large models, chips, data centres). Label: very large money and computing power. Upper floors shown faintly.

Explain.voiceover: Above that are tools for builders, which help other companies build with AI, for example by testing AI output or tracking costs. Then vertical AI, built for one industry, such as law, farming or dentistry. Vertical means going deep into one sector. At the top are applications, for general tasks like writing emails or editing photos.

slide.title: Four layers of AI startups
slide.body: Same building, upper floors revealed one by one: Tools for builders (customers are developers) · Vertical AI (one industry: law, farming, dentistry) · Applications (general tasks: emails, meeting notes, photos).

Explain.voiceover: Most applications and vertical products do not train their own model. They use a model from a model supplier, a company that offers a large model over the internet. The startup adds the rest: the screens, the instructions, the data, the connections to other tools, and customer support.

slide.title: What the startup adds
slide.body: Box at bottom: 'Model supplier (large model over the internet)'. Stacked on top in teal: screens · instructions to the model · data · connections to the customer's tools · customer support.

Explain.voiceover: Here is a picture to remember. In a city's food business, a few large companies run flour mills. That is infrastructure. Others sell ovens. Those are tools. A bakery that makes bread only for hospitals is vertical. A café that sells to anyone is an application.
Explain.stock_query: baker taking fresh bread from oven

Explain.voiceover: You do not need to own a flour mill to open a successful bakery. For a small team, vertical AI is often the best place to start, because it wins by knowing one industry better than anyone else.
Explain.on_screen_text: You don't need your own flour mill

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's meet three made up founders. Amara lives in Ghana. Farmers near her ask about pests and planting in local languages, but most advice online is in English.
Demonstrate.stock_query: small farmer using mobile phone in field

Demonstrate.voiceover: So she builds a phone service. Farmers send a voice note and get advice in their own language. This is vertical AI for farming. Her strength is not the model. It is her knowledge of local crops and languages, and her trust with farmer groups.

slide.title: Amara: vertical AI for farming
slide.body: Farmer's voice note (local language) → Amara's service → advice back in the same language. Side label: her strength = local crops, languages, trusted farmer groups.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Diego lives in Colombia. Small clinics lose hours each week writing appointment reminders and summarising patient forms. He builds a tool for clinic receptionists. That is also vertical AI. Because it touches health information, he must take data protection seriously, which we cover in lesson eleven.
Demonstrate.stock_query: receptionist at small medical clinic desk

Demonstrate.voiceover: Mei lives in Malaysia. Logistics companies ask her to read delivery documents that arrive in many formats. Later, other software developers want the same function inside their own products. So she considers selling it as a tool for builders.

slide.title: Mei: from vertical to tool
slide.body: Arrow from 'Document reading for logistics firms (vertical AI)' to 'Same function sold to developers (tool for builders)'. Caption: Mei · Malaysia.

Demonstrate.voiceover: None of the three trains a large model. All three add knowledge, data and relationships to existing models. And that brings us to a common mistake.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: No one trains a large model

Demonstrate.voiceover: Many new founders believe a real AI startup must build its own model. So they give up, or spend their first months and money on technology no customer asked for. Training a large model belongs to the infrastructure layer. For most founders, the valuable work is understanding a customer's problem deeply.

slide.title: Common mistake
slide.body: Left (red cross): 'A real AI startup builds its own model' → months and money spent, no customers. Right (green tick): 'Understand one customer problem deeply, use existing models'.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, the startup journey moves from idea to validation, MVP, product market fit and growth. Second, AI startups sit in four layers: infrastructure, tools for builders, vertical AI and applications. Third, a small team with little money usually has the best chance in vertical AI.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Idea → validation → MVP → product–market fit → growth. 2. Four layers: infrastructure, tools, vertical AI, applications. 3. Small teams: vertical AI and deep industry knowledge.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, list five AI startup ideas, classify each by layer, and mark the ones a two person team could start with little money. It takes about twenty minutes. Next, we look at finding a problem worth solving. See you there.
